newsitem.title: USA: Prosecutors score partial victory over Kevorkian.
newsitem.headline: Prosecutors score partial victory over Kevorkian.

text.p: Ionia County prosecutors scored a partial victory Wednesday against Dr. Jack Kevorkian when a judge allowed them to keep for now key evidence in a case involving a local woman who died in August.

Ionia County Circuit Judge Charles Miel also agreed to a prosecutor request to tighten Kevorkian's personal bond terms banning his presence at any more suicides -- but only for Ionia County in rural west-central Michigan.

Miel issued the rulings following a hearing Wednesday morning. Security at the Ionia County courthouse was tight, with about 25 city and county police officers guarding the courtroom and hallways following death threats against the assisted suicide crusader.

Kevorkian is charged with violating the state's "common law" ban on assisted suicide for helping Loretta Peabody, 54, die Aug. 30, 1996. The retired pathologist, who has publicly acknowledged attending 45 deaths since 1990, has been acquitted on similar charges in three separate trials.
Kevorkian did not attend the proceeding, after an arrangement was worked out between attorneys following two threating letters that were mailed recently to Ionia County Prosecutor Raymond Voet.

Miel rejected arguments from Kevorkian attorney Michael Schwartz that Ionia prosecutors had illegally seized a videotape in which Kevorkian is shown counselling Peabody, who suffered from multiple sclerosis.

After she died, Peabody's body was cremated and her death certificate was filled out to show she died of natural causes. But in September, Ionia prosecutors were made aware of the Peabody tape when police raided a hotel room in suburban Detroit and interrupted another Kevorkian counselling session.
Ionia authorities took the tape from Bloomfield Township Police Department in January after executing a search warrant.

After the hearing, Voet told reporters the tape is crucial to his case. Miel said during his ruling that whether the tape is admitted as evidence to the trial will be determined at a later date. He scheduled the trial to begin June 10.

Kevorkian has been free on a $10,000 personal bond since his November arrest, following his promise to not be present at any more assisted suicides. Earlier this month two women committed suicide, one who was left in Kevorkian's Volkswagen van, prompting Voet to seek more restrictive bond terms.
Kevorkian never admitted to being involved in the deaths. Miel issued a new bond order, but said it will only apply to Ionia County.
